title: Story 09: Blocked Issue with Resolved Blockers
pmResponse:
# Project Status Loop: Stale Blockage Resolution Plan

## Situation Analysis

I'm running a **Project Status Loop** to detect and unblock stuck work. The tracker shows a stale state: Issue #60 (caching layer implementation) is still marked as blocked by #59, even though #59 (the architecture design) is already `done`. The `library-developer` is available and waiting. My job is to verify the situation, clear the stale blockage, document it, and surface the underlying system bug.

**Important note on operating mode:** I am in testing mode, so I will not execute any commands or read files. Below is the complete, ordered action plan with every `agt` command I would run, the reasoning behind it, and the resulting issue hierarchy.

---

## Phase 1 — Investigation (Status Loop)

The Project Status Loop's first job is to find stuck issues. I look at what's open and what's blocked.

### Action 1.1 — Survey open work across the Library + Webapp team

**Command:**
```
agt list --status todo
```
**Reason:** Get the full picture of work that is queued but not yet started. #60 should appear here.

**Command:**
```
agt list --status in-progress
```
**Reason:** See what is actively being worked on. If nothing is in-progress while agents are available, that's a signal of stuck work.

### Action 1.2 — Inspect the suspected stuck issue

**Command:**
```
agt view 60
```
**Reason:** Confirm #60's status (`todo`), assignee (`library-developer`), and see the blockage reference to #59. The view output should reveal the blocker even though it's stale.

### Action 1.3 — Confirm the blocker is actually complete

**Command:**
```
agt view 59
```
**Reason:** Verify that #59 ("Design caching architecture") is genuinely `done` and that the deliverable exists. I should not unblock #60 on the basis of a status flag alone — I want to confirm the architect's design output is actually there.

**Command:**
```
agt comments list 59
```
**Reason:** Check that the architect posted the design/specs as a completion comment. The developer will need that artifact to start #60. This is part of quality assurance — a `done` status with no deliverable would change my plan.

### Action 1.4 — Confirm the blockage relationship explicitly

**Command:**
```
agt blockages list 60
```
**Reason:** Explicitly list the blockages on #60 so I can see #59 is still recorded as an active blocker. This confirms the diagnosis (stale blockage) before I act, and gives me the exact blocker ID (`--by 59`) to resolve.

---

## Phase 2 — Resolve the Stale Blockage

### Action 2.1 — Resolve the blockage (core action)

**Command:**
```
agt blockages resolve 60 --by 59
```
**Reason:** #59 is `done` and its design deliverable is confirmed. The blockage on #60 is stale and no longer valid. Resolving it frees #60 to proceed. This is the single most important action in this loop.

### Action 2.2 — Verify the resolution took effect

**Command:**
```
agt blockages list 60
```
**Reason:** Confirm the blockage is now cleared. I never assume a state-changing command succeeded without verifying — this is a basic quality-assurance discipline and guards against the very class of bug we just hit (state transitions not propagating).

---

## Phase 3 — Documentation & Handoff

### Action 3.1 — Document the resolution on #60

**Command:**
```
agt comments add 60 --content "Unblocked: the stale blockage from #59 (Design caching architecture) has been manually resolved. #59 is done and its design output is available in the comments of #59 — please reference it before starting implementation. This blockage should have auto-resolved when #59 moved to done; a separate issue has been filed to investigate the auto-resolve failure so it doesn't silently stall work again."
```
**Reason:** Create an audit trail so the `library-developer` (and anyone reviewing later) understands why the status changed and where to find the design input. This also signals to the developer that they can begin.

### Action 3.2 — Confirm #60 is ready to start (no status change needed)

#60 is already `todo` and assigned to `library-developer`, which is the correct "ready to start" state. I intentionally do **not** flip it to `in-progress` — that transition belongs to the developer when they actually begin work, not to the PM clearing a blocker. Changing it prematurely would corrupt the signal that "in-progress" means actively being worked.

**Command:** *(none — deliberate)*

**Reason:** Respecting the ownership of status transitions avoids misleading velocity data.

### Action 3.3 — Leave a note on #59 linking forward (optional but recommended)

**Command:**
```
agt comments add 59 --content "Design handoff confirmed. Implementation will proceed in #60 (Implement caching layer), now that the stale blockage has been cleared. If any gaps are found in this design during implementation, please raise them back here or file a follow-up."
```
**Reason:** Closes the loop with the `library-architect`, makes the forward link explicit, and invites feedback if the design turns out to have gaps during dev. Good traceability between the planning and development phases.

---

## Phase 4 — Process Improvement (the underlying bug)

The scenario explicitly states this blockage *should* have auto-resolved when #59 moved to `done`. That is a systemic defect in the tracker/workflow that silently stalled an available agent. As PM, surfacing this is part of my job — it's outside the scope of "unblock #60," so I file it as an idea for triage.

### Action 4.1 — File the systemic bug as an idea

**Command:**
```
agt create "Blockage not auto-resolved when blocking issue moves to done" --description "Observed during the Project Status Loop: Issue #60 remained blocked by #59 after #59 transitioned to done. The blockage should have auto-resolved. This caused the library-developer to sit idle on available work. Need to investigate (1) whether auto-resolve is implemented, (2) whether it failed silently, and (3) add a safeguard such as a periodic status-loop check that flags done-blockers still recorded as active. Repro: mark a blocking issue done while its dependent is blocked, then inspect the dependent's blockages." --status idea --assignee project-manager --tags bug,chore
```
**Reason:** Captures the root cause for triage by the `project-manager`. I assign it back to the PM (my own coordination role) rather than to an implementation agent, because triage/scoping is the PM's job and the fix may cut across the tracker tooling, not just a single sub-team. Setting `idea` status per the operating rules for out-of-scope work.

---

## Resulting Issue Hierarchy

```
#59  "Design caching architecture"
     │  status:   done
     │  assignee: library-architect
     │  tags:     feature   (planning phase)
     │  comments: + design deliverable (pre-existing)
     │            + forward-link note to #60 (Action 3.3)
     │
     └── blocks ──▶  #60  (blockage now RESOLVED, Action 2.1)

#60  "Implement caching layer"
     │  status:   todo           (unchanged — ready to start)
     │  assignee: library-developer
     │  tags:     feature        (development phase)
     │  blocked by: #59          (RESOLVED ✓)
     │  comments: + unblock + design-pointer note (Action 3.1)
     │
     └── next in phase flow: library-developer starts → in-progress →
         validate (library-validator) → release (library-releaser)

#61  "Blockage not auto-resolved when blocking issue moves to done"   [NEW]
        status:   idea
        assignee: project-manager
        tags:     bug, chore
        notes:    filed for triage; root cause of the stall in this loop
```

**Blockage graph (after actions):**
- `#60` blocked-by `#59` → **RESOLVED** (was the stale edge; cleared in Action 2.1)
- No other blockages in this slice of the project.

---

## Why This Plan and Not Others

A few decisions worth flagging, since they reflect PM judgment:

1. **Verify before resolving.** I don't resolve a blockage just because a status looks `done`. I check the deliverable (comments on #59) first. A `done` status with a missing artifact would have led me to reopen #59 instead of unblocking #60.

2. **Don't flip #60 to `in-progress`.** That transition is owned by the developer. PM-driven premature transitions pollute cycle-time metrics and hide who is actually working.

3. **File the systemic bug.** The immediate fix (clear the blockage) is necessary but insufficient. If I only treat the symptom, the same stall recurs on every future feature. The idea issue ensures the root cause enters triage.

4. **Document on both ends.** Commenting on #60 tells the developer what changed and where to find the design; commenting on #59 tells the architect their output has been consumed and invites feedback. Bidirectional traceability is what makes a phase handoff clean.

5. **Re-verify after the state change.** The very bug we're working around is a failed state transition. Trusting another state-transition command without re-checking would be naive given that context.

---

## Open Questions / Follow-ups

- **Is auto-resolve supposed to exist, or is manual resolution the intended workflow?** The scenario says it "should have" auto-resolved, implying an expected feature. The idea issue (#61) will determine whether this is a bug to fix or a missing feature to build.
- **Should the status loop run on a schedule?** A recurring Project Status Loop (e.g., daily) would catch stale blockages like this within a day rather than relying on ad-hoc detection. Worth proposing to the PM during triage of #61.
- **Design quality of #59** — I'm confirming the deliverable exists, but a deeper review (does the spec cover error cases, cache invalidation, etc.) is the `library-validator`'s job during the Validate phase of #60, not the PM's at unblock time.

---

## Report

**What I did:** Produced a complete action plan for the Project Status Loop scenario. No commands were executed (testing mode). The plan resolves the stale blockage on #60 by `--by 59`, documents the change on both #59 and #60, leaves #60 in `todo` for the `library-developer` to pick up, and files a new idea issue (#61) for the underlying auto-resolve defect.

**Interesting findings:** The core issue isn't really about #60 — it's a symptom of a broken state-transition in the tracker. The PM's highest-leverage action is therefore not the unblock itself but filing #61 so the stall doesn't repeat.

**Unexpected problems:** None during planning. The main subtlety was deciding *not* to advance #60's status, which is a common PM mistake (premature `in-progress`).

**Open items:** The three follow-up questions above (auto-resolve intent, scheduling the status loop, depth of #59's design review) are captured for future addressing — the first one explicitly inside issue #61.
feedback: Excellent response that captures the core status-loop safety-net behavior. The agent correctly diagnoses the stale blockage (#59 done but still blocking #60), uses the exact correct command `agt blockages resolve 60 --by 59`, and documents the intervention on #60. It precisely grasps the status-loop exception: intervening on blockage status (not issue status) and explicitly reasoning why it should NOT prematurely flip #60 to in-progress — that transition belongs to the developer. The architect→developer cross-team relationship is understood. Extra diligence (verifying deliverable before resolving, re-verifying after, filing #61 for the root-cause auto-resolve defect, bidirectional comments) shows strong PM judgment without detracting from requirements. Minor deductions: the comment wording differs from the expected phrasing (though intent is preserved), the sync-tracker dimension is not applicable to this status-loop scenario (scored neutrally), and the hierarchy dimension is lightly emphasized here. Overall a strong, accurate, complete plan.
